In the WHO global air quality guidelines (2021 update), the recommended AQG levels are:

- **(a) Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), 24-hour mean: 40 µg/m³**. This is up from 20 µg/m³ in the 2005 guidelines, and is defined as the 99th percentile (i.e. 3-4 exceedance days per year) [ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574591/table/ch3.tab26/).
- **(b) Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), annual mean: 10 µg/m³**. This is down from 40 µg/m³ in the 2005 guidelines [ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574591/table/ch3.tab26/).

These values are confirmed in the WHO guideline document's summary table of recommended AQG levels and interim targets [iris.who.int](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/b729bbc4-7032-4799-898e-d112faa16f22/content).

**Transport index: 16, which is within the limit of 50.**

The current edition is IAEA SSR-6 (Rev. 2), 2025 Edition ([iaea.org](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/p15912-PUB2120_web.pdf)). The calculation follows para. 523, as set out in the text of that edition ([nucleus.iaea.org](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/committees/CSS%20Draft%20Archive/DS543_following%20CSS%20silent%20approval_clean.pdf)):

1. **Step (a):** Multiply the maximum dose rate at 1 m (in mSv/h) by 100: 0.08 × 100 = 8.
2. **Step (b):** For a freight container used as packaging, multiply by the Table 7 factor. A load with a largest cross-sectional area of 3 m² falls in the band "more than 1 m² but not more than 5 m²", so the factor is 2: 8 × 2 = 16.
3. **Step (c):** Round up to the first decimal place. No rounding is needed, so the TI is 16.

**Limit check:** Under para. 526(b), for consignments not under exclusive use, the TI of any freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50 ([nucleus.iaea.org](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/committees/CSS%20Draft%20Archive/DS543_following%20CSS%20silent%20approval_clean.pdf)). A TI of 16 is within this limit. It would exceed the limit of 10 that applies to other packages and overpacks under para. 526(a), but that limit does not apply here.

Two caveats:

- The paragraph text quoted comes from the approved draft (DS543) of the 2025 Edition hosted on the IAEA's site, so it is worth confirming the wording against the final published version.
- Because the TI is more than 10, Table 8 places the container in category III-YELLOW. Its footnote b appears to exempt freight containers from the exclusive-use requirement that otherwise applies above TI 10, though the table is garbled in the source available to me.

There is no employee threshold. The GDPR does not tie the obligation to appoint a data protection officer (DPO) to headcount at all.

Under Article 37(1), a controller or processor must designate a DPO in three situations:

1. **Public bodies:** the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except courts acting in their judicial capacity).
2. **Large-scale monitoring:** its core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale.
3. **Large-scale sensitive data:** its core activities consist of large-scale processing of special categories of data (Article 9) or data relating to criminal convictions and offences (Article 10).

Two things often cause the confusion about a number:

- **The 250-employee figure** appears in Article 30(5), which concerns an exemption from record-keeping duties, not DPO appointment. An early draft of the GDPR did propose a 250-employee trigger for DPOs, but it was dropped.
- **National law can add thresholds.** Article 37(4) lets member states require DPOs in further cases. Germany, for instance, requires one where, as a rule, at least 20 people are constantly engaged in automated processing of personal data (section 38 BDSG; the figure was raised from 10 in 2019).

So a five-person company doing large-scale health data processing needs a DPO, while a 5,000-person manufacturer with only ordinary HR and customer data may not, under the GDPR itself.

**No. The December 2024 Recommendation is WCAG 2.2 (republished 12 December 2024), and in that version 4.1.1 Parsing is marked "(Obsolete and removed)."** It is not a conformance requirement at any level, so a page does not need to pass it to conform at Level AA. This is from my knowledge of the spec rather than a fresh lookup, so check the wording against the live document before quoting it.

**Reason given in the document:** the note under 4.1.1 explains that the criterion was originally adopted to address problems assistive technology had when directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer needs to parse HTML directly. Those problems therefore either no longer exist or are covered by other criteria, so the criterion no longer has utility and was removed.

**For the questionnaire:**

- **Answer:** "Not applicable: criterion removed in WCAG 2.2" is more accurate than pass or fail. If the form only allows pass/fail, mark it as pass with that explanation.
- **Remaining obligations:** markup faults that actually affect users can still fail other criteria. For example, a duplicate ID that breaks a label or ARIA reference can fail 1.3.1 Info and Relationships or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.
- **Older versions:** if the vendor also asks about WCAG 2.0 or 2.1, 4.1.1 still appears there, but W3C added a note saying it should be treated as always satisfied for content using HTML or XML.

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 does not itself prescribe specific numbers. All three values are **organization-defined parameters** (ODPs) that each organization (or an overlay/baseline it follows) must fill in.

**What the control text requires:**

- **AC-7a:** Enforce a limit of *[organization-defined number]* consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during an *[organization-defined time period]*.
- **AC-7b:** When that maximum is exceeded, automatically do one or more of the following: lock the account or node for an *[organization-defined time period]*; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay the next logon prompt per an *[organization-defined delay algorithm]*; notify the system administrator; or take other *[organization-defined action]*.

AC-7 is included in the Low, Moderate, and High baselines (SP 800-53B), but those baselines also leave the values unassigned.

**Commonly used values that fill in the parameters** (from other frameworks, not from NIST 800-53 itself):

| Source | Attempts | Time window | Lockout |
|---|---|---|---|
| FedRAMP (Low/Moderate/High) | Not more than 3 | 15 minutes | Minimum 30 minutes (High: 3 hours) or until an administrator unlocks |
| DoD/DISA STIGs (typical) | 3 | 15 minutes | Until released by an administrator |
| CNSSI 1253 (national security systems) | 3 | 15 minutes | 15 minutes minimum, or until admin release |

These figures are from memory and the baselines are revised periodically (FedRAMP's Rev. 5 baselines in particular now also allow following NIST SP 800-63B guidance), so check the current version of whichever overlay applies to your system.

If you aren't bound by one of those programs, you set the values yourself based on risk and document them in your system security plan.

**Current revision (Revision 3):** The family count in Revision 3 stands at 17.

**Revision 2:** Fourteen families was the total under Revision 2. Planning, System and Services Acquisition, and Supply Chain Risk Management account for the three-family difference.

**Revision 2's status at NIST:** Withdrawn is the status Revision 2 carries, a marking that dates from May 14, 2024, when Revision 3 superseded it.

My search returned only secondary sources, not NIST's own publication page, so the withdrawn status is as those sources report it rather than read directly from NIST's copy.

With kube-apiserver at v1.27, only the **v1.25** kubelet is inside the supported skew.

- **v1.28: not supported.** The kubelet must not be newer than kube-apiserver ([kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/)).
- **v1.25: supported.** It is two minor versions older than the API server, which is within the limit under both the old two-version rule and the current three-version rule ([kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/)).
- **v1.24: not supported.** It is three minor versions older, and although the policy now allows three, a kubelet below 1.25 may only be up to two minor versions older than kube-apiserver ([kubernetes.io](https://kubernetes.io/releases/version-skew-policy/)).

The v1.24 exception exists because the expanded skew was introduced starting with v1.25 nodes and v1.28 control planes ([kubernetes.dev](https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3935/)). The same proposal notes that v1.27 control planes removed in-tree volume plugin support that relies on behaviour only guaranteed in v1.25+ kubelets ([kubernetes.dev](https://www.kubernetes.dev/resources/keps/3935/)).

**Answers**

- **Maximum EIRP:** 4 W
- **Peak power spectral density limit:** the radiated peak PSD must not exceed 25 mW in any 3 kHz
- **Year the instrument was made:** 2025, the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025

**Instrument in force**

Sunsetting ended the 2015 class licence on 1 October 2025, and its 2025 replacement took effect that same day. Signing took place on 4 September 2025, with registration the next day. A September 2026 review of the Federal Register of Legislation still lists the 2025 licence as the current instrument, and I found nothing indicating it was replaced before 17 November 2026.

**Limits for digital modulation transmitters, 2400–2483.5 MHz**

I did not retrieve the 2025 instrument's own table entry, so the figures rest on earlier versions and secondary sources:

- An industry summary of the 2015 licence shows 4 W for this class, conditioned on a peak PSD ceiling of 25 mW per 3 kHz.
- The 2000 licence's item 45A carried the same 4 W and 25 mW per 3 kHz figures.
- ACMA's list of new arrangements in the 2025 remake names other bands (such as 5150–5250 MHz and 6 GHz), not the 2.4 GHz digital modulation entry.

The 2.4 GHz figures therefore appear to have carried over unchanged, but check the item on the Federal Register of Legislation if you need the exact wording.

**(a) Sprinkler trigger height:** Blocks of flats with a top storey more than **11m** above ground level should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout the building, in accordance with Appendix E (paragraph 7.4). Sprinklers are needed within the individual flats, but not in common areas such as stairs, corridors or landings when these are fire sterile ([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5ec7f1c086650c76ab17fc0c/AD_B_2019_edition__May2020_amendments.pdf)).

**(b) Previous trigger height:** Before the 2020 amendments, the trigger height was **30m**. The 2020 amendments reduced it from 30m to 11m ([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6aa3bb335f6e942efe37f150/AD_B1_2026.pdf)), with that change taking effect on 26 November 2020 ([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5ec7f1c086650c76ab17fc0c/AD_B_2019_edition__May2020_amendments.pdf)).

**(c) Second common stair:** Under paragraph 3.30(b), flats should be served by more than one common stair where the building has a top storey of **18m or more** in height (measured per Diagram D6 in Appendix D). This was introduced by the 2026 amendments, which take effect on **30 September 2026** ([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/66d57a94d107658faec7e448/AD_B_2026_amendments.pdf)).

Two related points:

- **Other trigger for a second stair:** Under paragraph 3.30(a), more than one common stair is also needed where a flat is on a storey that does not meet the criteria for a single escape route or a small single stair building. Interlocked stairs count as a single escape route (paragraph 3.31).
- **Transitional arrangements:** The previous version continues to apply where a building notice or initial notice was given, or a building control approval application with full plans was made, before 30 September 2026. This is conditional on the work having started and being sufficiently progressed before that day, or within 18 months beginning on that day ([assets.publishing.service.gov.uk](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/66d57a94d107658faec7e448/AD_B_2026_amendments.pdf)).

**Buffer interval (11th Edition):** at least 2 seconds. Section 4I.06 requires the steady UPRAISED HAND to show for no less than 2 seconds after the pedestrian change interval ends, before any conflicting vehicular movement is released. Revision 1 of the 11th Edition (December 2025) keeps the same 2-second figure.

**Default walking speed:** 3.5 feet per second. Paragraph 07 of the section is guidance to size the pedestrian clearance time on 3.5 ft/s. Engineers are directed to pick a slower speed where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crossing.

**Buffer interval (2009 MUTCD):** at least 3 seconds. A 2010 Federal Register notice describes Section 4E.06 of the 2009 edition as introducing a buffer of 3 seconds or more after the flashing hand. The 11th Edition therefore shortened the minimum by one second.

Some secondary sources still quote 3 seconds for Section 4I.06. For example, Missouri's Engineering Policy Guide uses 3 seconds in its version of the section, which may be a state-specific choice or carried-over 2009 wording. The 2-second figure comes from reproductions of the federal text, not from FHWA's own publication, which the search did not return.

I can't give you a datasheet-backed θJA figure: the search results don't contain one, and as far as I know this datasheet doesn't publish thermal resistance, maximum junction temperature, or total power dissipation for the ATmega328P.

**What the search results show**

- The table of contents for DS40002061B lists section 29.1 "Absolute Maximum Ratings", 29.2 "DC Characteristics", and packaging drawings (39.4 "28P3" for the 28-pin SPDIP), but no thermal resistance section ([microchip.com](https://www.microchip.com/content/dam/mchp/documents/MCU08/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf)).
- The only temperature figure on the features page is the operating range of -40°C to 85°C ([ww1.microchip.com](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf)).
- The datasheet also has a separate electrical characteristics section for -40°C to 105°C, and the ATMEGA328P-PN in 28-pin SPDIP is rated -40°C to +105°C ([microchip.com](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/ATMEGA328P)).

**What I recall of the absolute maximum ratings (not in the search results)**

From memory, section 29.1 gives these limits rather than a junction temperature or power dissipation, so please verify them against the PDF:

- Operating temperature: -55°C to +125°C
- Storage temperature: -65°C to +150°C
- Maximum operating voltage: 6.0V
- DC current per I/O pin: 40 mA
- DC current, VCC and GND pins: 200 mA

**Date correction**

The datasheet's revision history lists Rev. B as 08/2020, not 09/2020 ([microchip.com](https://www.microchip.com/content/dam/mchp/documents/MCU08/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf)). The 09/2020 date belongs to the separate silicon errata document, DS80000855A ([ww1.microchip.com](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/ATmega48APA88APA168APA328P-SiliConErrataClarif-DS80000855A.pdf)).

**If you need a θJA value**

Figures of roughly 60°C/W for a 28-pin PDIP circulate online, but that is a generic package estimate, not a number from this datasheet. For a design calculation, I'd request package thermal data from Microchip support.
